query: For high-entropy-alloy materials intended for self-lubricating moving components, what single intervention could reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate across a wide service-temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites prior evidence supporting it, and proposes an experiment whose outcome could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Incorporating a controlled amount of Mo (around 5–10 wt%, e.g. ~7 wt%) into the HEA will induce the in situ formation of a lubricious MoO2 layer during sliding in an oxygen‐rich environment, thereby reducing both the coefficient of friction and wear rate across a broad service-temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: A self-lubricating HEA produced without specialized additive elements, which typically exhibits high friction (≈0.7) and elevated wear rates under high-temperature and high-load conditions.
generation.intervention: Introduce a precisely controlled Mo addition (targeting ~7 wt% based on prior optimization studies) either by alloying or via coating modification.
generation.conditions: Tested under ambient to elevated temperatures (room temperature up to ~800 °C) with moderate to high loads, ensuring an oxygen-rich friction environment to promote MoO2 formation.
generation.structural_mediator: In situ precipitation of a fine, uniformly distributed MoO2 phase at grain boundaries and worn surface sites.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, Mo in the alloy reacts with ambient oxygen to form a thin, layered MoO2 film. The lubricious MoO2 layer, with weak interlayer bonding, reduces shear forces and direct metal-metal contact, while concurrently the inherent alloy hardness limits wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in the friction coefficient (potentially over 50% lower than untreated HEA) and an order-of-magnitude decrease in wear rate across the service-temperature range.
generation.baseline: Untreated HEAs typically exhibit friction coefficients around 0.7 and higher wear rates under comparable conditions.
generation.boundary: The lubricious effect critically depends on maintaining Mo levels within the optimal range; excessive Mo may induce unwanted phase transformations or embrittlement, and oxygen availability must remain sufficient to promote MoO2 formation. Extreme temperatures beyond 800 °C may alter oxide stability.
generation.uncertainty: While MoO2 formation is well-supported by prior evidence, the exact quantitative impact across all temperature ranges and under varying oxygen partial pressures still requires detailed in situ tribological and phase analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one with the optimized ~7 wt% Mo addition and a baseline without Mo. Conduct ball-on-disk friction tests in an oxygen-rich environment over 25–800 °C and under variable loads, while monitoring surface oxide evolution using XPS and XRD.
measurements: Surface phase analysis (XRD, XPS, TEM) to detect and quantify MoO2 formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Mo-incorporated samples do not consistently exhibit lower friction and reduced wear relative to the baseline, or if a stable and lubricious MoO2 film is absent under the test conditions, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The results reveal that the Mo content significantly affects the microstructure, hardness, fracture toughness, and tribological behavior of the coatings. As the Mo content in the coatings increases gradually, the preferred orientation changes from (200) to (111). The coatings consistently exhibit a distinct columnar structure.
